newsitem.title: USA: Gore-Kemp debate may give glimpse of 2000 campaign.
newsitem.headline: Gore-Kemp debate may give glimpse of 2000 campaign.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Vice President Al Gore and Republican Jack Kemp square off in a debate on Wednesday that has political junkies aflutter at the thought that these two may compete for the presidency in the year 2000.
Vice presidential debates have had little impact on presidential elections and Wednesday's 90-minute encounter in St Petersburg, Florida, is expected to be no exception.
Still, the stakes are unusually high since both Gore and Kemp are seen as strong early bets for the Democratic and Republican presidential nominations for the next election.

"It is very unusual for a debate to showcase the two possible nominees of four years down the road, but both Gore and Kemp are undoubtedly the early frontrunners," said Allan Lichtman, a political scientist at American University in Washington.

That makes the debate possibly of more interest to political analysts, pundits and journalists than to the electorate, who are focusing on the contest between President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole.
Those two meet in the final presidential debate next week in San Diego. The election is November 5 and Clinton remains ahead in the opinion polls.

Even in Florida, the vice presidential contest is only getting big media play in the Tampa-St Petersburg metropolitan area, said Robert Joffee, a Florida public opinion expert with the Mason-Dixon polling company.

"The vice presidential debate has no significance at all for the presidential election. On the other hand, every political junkie in America, justifiably, will be watching this with a great deal of interest for 2000," said Joffee.
It is possible, however, that the debate may have some impact in Florida, a traditionally Republican state where Clinton has a narrow lead mainly due to the support of women.
Joffee said Kemp's favourability rating was substantially better than Dole's in Florida, while Clinton and Gore both enjoyed about the same level of support.
If Kemp could help Dole in Florida alone, he would be doing the Republican nominee a big favour.
Past vice presidential debates have often seen the contestants take on attack-dog roles as surrogates for their running-mates, who are usually wary about seeming overly harsh in their own debates.
In 1992, Gore and then-Vice President Dan Quayle went at each other no-holds-barred in their one debate.
That is not likely to be the case this time with both contestants looking to the future. Gore and Kemp may wish to look presidential and avoid gaffes that could haunt them.
The stakes are especially high for Gore, who has a spotty record in debates and has to overcome a reputation for being dull and wooden.

After a rocky showing against Quayle in 1992, he came back in a televised debate on the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1993 and performed strongly against NAFTA critic Ross Perot, in the view of many who watched those debates.

Kemp, who was a star on the inspirational speaker circuit before Dole picked him as his running mate, has less to prove. His problem can be a tendency to talk too much about subjects that enthuse him.

The former football star's political career seemed over before Dole surprised the political world by selecting him in August. But Kemp has proved highly popular among Republicans and has won high marks for his energetic performance on the campaign trail, taking the Republican message to the inner cities and to black voters usually ignored by the party.
"Kemp will start the race for the Republican nomination in 2000 slightly ahead in quite a strong and deep field," said Lichtman. "Gore has fewer potential challengers for the Democratic nomination."
